chapter_theme: Pazhamudircholai (பழமுதிர்சோலை, 2 of 2): one song in which the poet, describing lovemaking, vows that even sunk in that old infatuation he will not forget Murugan's garlanded crown and the vel in his hand; the praise names Uma's son, the vel of knowledge thrown at Sura's hill and sea, and the lord of Kulagiri.

1322.reading: The poet describes lovemaking on a flower bed, cloud-dark hair loosened, scent and sweat mingling, crescent brows turning, garments slipping, breasts heaving and faces pressed together, and says that even while he is sunk and rejoicing in that old infatuation he will not forget Murugan's crown swaying with garlands, his form and the vel in his hand. The praise names him son of Uma of the bow brows, half of Siva, green-gold of body, the Murugan of knowledge who with a small smile hurled the vel so that Sura's hill and sea burned, Valli's bridegroom with the kadamba garland, at Kulagiri.
1322.nuance: Unusually there is no plea to be freed from desire: மகிழ்கினும் ... மறவேனே, 'even while I rejoice, I will not forget'. The remembrance of the god is held inside the confession rather than set against it. The vel is called ஞான, knowledge, as it is elsewhere.

links.note: The Kural's lover says he would remember her if he forgot, but மறப்பறியேன், he does not know how to forget. The Thiruppugazh says that even while sunk in love-play, மகிழ்கினும் ... முடிவடிவொடு அங்கை வேலும் மறவேனே, he will not forget Murugan's crowned form and the vel in his hand. The same claim of never forgetting moves from the beloved to the god, and in the song it holds even in the middle of desire.
